nameStory: Summer snowflake gets its charming name from its pristine white flowers that dangle like tiny snowbells, creating the illusion of fresh snow even in the warmer months. The scientific name Leucojum comes from Greek words meaning "white violet," though it's not related to violets at all! It's also called St. Agnes' flower, named after the patron saint of virgins and gardeners.
description: Summer snowflake is a graceful bulbous plant that produces clusters of nodding, bell-shaped white flowers on slender green stems. Each delicate flower is about half an inch long and hangs like a tiny lantern from the stem. The plant grows from an underground bulb and reaches about 12-18 inches tall, with narrow, strap-like green leaves that emerge in a clump. It belongs to the amaryllis family, making it a cousin to daffodils and onions.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Pure white, bell-shaped flowers that nod downward like tiny snowbells, each with 6 petals that often have small green spots at the tips. The flowers feel papery and delicate to the touch.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Narrow, strap-like leaves that emerge in a clump from the base, resembling thick grass blades but with a smooth, waxy texture when you run your fingers along them.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms neat clumps 12-18 inches tall, growing from underground bulbs that feel firm and onion-like if carefully dug up.

idTips.label: Stem
idTips.description: Smooth, hollow green flower stems that feel sturdy but bend easily, typically bearing 2-5 drooping flowers in a loose cluster at the top.

habitat: Summer snowflake thrives in moist, rich soils and is most commonly found in partially shaded areas like woodland edges, old gardens, and naturalized areas around historic properties. In New England, look for it in damp meadows, along stream banks, or in areas where old homesteads once stood, as it often persists long after gardens are abandoned.

seasonality.spring: Bright green leaves emerge early, followed by the distinctive white bell flowers that bloom from late April through May, filling the air with a subtle, sweet fragrance.
seasonality.summer: After flowering, the leaves remain green and photosynthetic, slowly building energy reserves in the underground bulb for next year's display.
seasonality.fall: Leaves begin to yellow and die back, marking the plant's retreat underground where the bulb will remain dormant.
seasonality.winter: Completely dormant with no above-ground parts visible, existing only as a bulb buried safely below the frost line.

funFact: Despite being called "summer" snowflake, this plant actually blooms in late spring - it got its name to distinguish it from its earlier-blooming cousin, spring snowflake, which flowers even earlier in the year!
confusionNotes: Summer snowflake is most easily confused with spring snowflake, but summer snowflake is taller, blooms later, and has multiple flowers per stem versus spring snowflake's typically single flower per stem. Remember: "Summer snowflake = Several flowers" for the alliteration!
contextualKnowledge: Summer snowflake is native to Europe but has naturalized in parts of New England, often marking sites of old homesteads where it was originally planted in gardens. It's one of only two species left in the genus Leucojum, as botanists have moved most former snowflake species into a different genus called Acis.
compareHints: Summer snowflake differs from its only close relative in New England, spring snowflake, by blooming later in the season, growing taller, and producing multiple drooping flowers per stem rather than just one. Spring snowflake is also much less common in our region, making summer snowflake the snowflake you're most likely to encounter in New England gardens and naturalized areas.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Spring snowflake differs from its close relative, summer snowflake (Leucojum aestivum), primarily by blooming time and size - spring snowflake blooms in early spring and stays under 8 inches tall, while summer snowflake blooms in late spring to early summer and can reach 18 inches tall.
